documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: Problem 4
problems.statement:
When two hydrogen atoms come together, the $1s$ atomic orbitals combine to form bonding and anti-bonding molecular orbitals.

![](p4-fig1)

In a similar way, we may combine the atomic orbitals of more complicated atoms to form molecular orbitals, taking into account the symmetry of the molecule. Consider the ozone molecule, $\mathrm{O_3}$, shaped like an Australian boomerang. Arrange the oxygens in the $yz$ plane and assume $1s,2s,2p_x,2p_y,2p_z$ orbitals on each atom.

![](p4-fig2)

Atoms $\mathrm{O_a}$ and $\mathrm{O_c}$ are related by symmetry. Their $1s$ orbitals form symmetric and anti-symmetric combinations.

![](p4-fig3)

The $1s$ atomic orbital on $\mathrm{O_b}$ is classified as symmetric. It can combine with the symmetric combination of $\mathrm{O_a}$ and $\mathrm{O_c}$, but not with the anti-symmetric combination, to form bonding and anti-bonding molecular orbitals. The anti-symmetric combination is non-bonding. The final three molecular orbitals follow.

![](p4-fig4)

sections.title: Molecular orbitals and geometry

parts.statement:
On the answer sheet, use a similar approach to construct the molecular orbitals arising from the separate interaction of the $2s,2p_x,2p_y,2p_z$ atomic orbitals. Remember to form the symmetric and anti-symmetric combinations of $\mathrm{O_a}$ and $\mathrm{O_c}$ first.

We may rearrange these molecular orbitals in order of increasing energy. This can be generalized to other triatomic molecules. Orbital energies differ between bent triatomic molecules such as ozone and linear molecules such as carbon dioxide. Their variation may be represented in a Walsh diagram for $\mathrm{XY_2}$ molecules, shown on the answer sheet: orbital energy versus the Y–X–Y bond angle. The labels are called symmetry labels. The $6a_1$ orbital referred to in that diagram is shown below.

![](p4-fig5)

Why does the energy of the $6a_1$ orbital increase so rapidly as the bond angle changes from $90^\circ$ to $180^\circ$?

Only occupied molecular orbitals affect the geometry, and a doubly occupied orbital has more influence than a singly occupied orbital. For example, $\mathrm{O_3}$ has 24 electrons, so at $135^\circ$ the orbitals are doubly occupied up to $6a_1$. The lowest-energy geometry of ozone, taking into account steric repulsion and the contrasting energy behaviour of the $4b_2,1a_2,6a_1$ orbitals, is probably towards the left of the Walsh diagram, consistent with the observed angle of $116^\circ$.
At a bond angle of $135^\circ$, what are the highest occupied orbitals for $\mathrm{BO_2,CO_2,NO_2,FO_2}$?

The bond angles of $\mathrm{BO_2,CO_2,O_3}$ are experimentally $180^\circ,180^\circ,116^\circ$, respectively. Use the Walsh diagram on the answer sheet to predict whether $\mathrm{NO_2}$ and $\mathrm{FO_2}$ are more or less bent than $\mathrm{O_3}$.

sections.statement:
Construction of the molecular orbitals arising from the separate interaction of the $2s,2p_x,2p_y,2p_z$ atomic orbitals is shown in the native diagram. Its complete orbital signs, axes, atom combinations and five orbital groups are retained.

![](p4-sol-fig1)

The key repeats the question and gives these choices:

- a) Because the bonding character decreases.
- b) Because the anti-bonding character increases.
- c) Both (a) and (b).
- d) Because the overlap decreases.

The correct answer is **c**. The energy changes rapidly because the overlap is bonding between all three atoms in the bent molecule, but becomes increasingly anti-bonding as the molecule approaches linearity.

The native boxes print:

| Molecule | Highest occupied orbital and electron count |
| --- | --- |
| $\mathrm{O_3}$ | $6a_x$ (24 $e^-$) |
| $\mathrm{BO_2}$ | $4b_2$ (21 $e^-$) |
| $\mathrm{CO_2}$ | $4b_2$ (22 $e^-$) |
| $\mathrm{NO_2}$ | $6a_1$ (23 $e^-$) |
| $\mathrm{FO_2}$ | $2b_x$ (25 $e^-$) |
The correct answer is **(d)**: $\mathrm{NO_2}$ is less bent than $\mathrm{O_3}$, and $\mathrm{FO_2}$ is more bent than $\mathrm{O_3}$.

problems.title: Problem 5
problems.statement: Metallic gold is frequently finely dispersed among other minerals in aluminosilicate rocks. It may be extracted by treating crushed rock with aerated sodium cyanide solution. Gold slowly becomes water-soluble $\mathrm{[Au(CN)_2]^-}$ (reaction 1). After equilibrium, the aqueous phase is pumped off. Metallic gold is recovered by reacting its complex with zinc, converted to $\mathrm{[Zn(CN)_4]^{2-}}$ (reaction 2).

sections.title: Gold extraction

parts.statement:
Write balanced ionic equations for reactions 1 and 2.

Gold in nature is frequently alloyed with silver, also oxidized by aerated sodium cyanide.

A 500 L solution, $0.0100\ \mathrm{M}$ in $\mathrm{[Au(CN)_2]^-}$ and $0.0030\ \mathrm{M}$ in $\mathrm{[Ag(CN)_2]^-}$, was evaporated to one third of its original volume and treated with zinc (40 g). Assuming deviation from standard conditions is unimportant and all these redox reactions essentially go to completion, calculate the concentrations of both complexes after reaction ceases.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{[Zn(CN)_4]^{2-}+2e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Zn+4CN^-},&E^\circ&=-1.26\ \mathrm{V},\\
\mathrm{[Au(CN)_2]^-+e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Au+2CN^-},&E^\circ&=-0.60\ \mathrm{V},\\
\mathrm{[Ag(CN)_2]^-+e^-}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ag+2CN^-},&E^\circ&=-0.31\ \mathrm{V}.
\end{aligned}
$$
$\mathrm{[Au(CN)_2]^-}$ is very stable under certain conditions. What sodium cyanide concentration is required to keep 99 mol% of gold in solution as the cyanide complex? $K_f=4\times10^{28}$.
There have been several efforts to develop alternative gold extraction processes. Why? Choose one option on the answer sheet.

sections.statement:
$$
\mathrm{4Au+8CN^-+O_2+2H_2O\longrightarrow4[Au(CN)_2]^-+4OH^-},
$$

$$
\mathrm{Zn+2[Au(CN)_2]^-\longrightarrow[Zn(CN)_4]^{2-}+2Au}.
$$

$$
E^\circ(\mathrm{Ag/Zn})=-0.31-(-1.26)=0.95\ \mathrm{V},\qquad
E^\circ(\mathrm{Au/Zn})=-0.60-(-1.26)=0.66\ \mathrm{V}.
$$

Since the Ag/Zn value is larger, the Ag(I) complex is reduced first. Amounts in 500 dm³:

$$
n(\mathrm{Ag(I)})=500(0.0030)=1.5\ \mathrm{mol},\quad
n(\mathrm{Au(I)})=500(0.010)=5.0\ \mathrm{mol},\quad
n(\mathrm{Zn})=40/65.38=0.61\ \mathrm{mol}.
$$

One mole zinc reacts with two moles Ag(I) or Au(I); 0.61 mol Zn consumes 1.2 mol silver complex. Remaining silver complex is $1.5-1.2=0.3$ mol; the gold complex is not reduced.

$$
[\mathrm{Au(CN)_2^-}]=0.010(3)=0.030\ \mathrm{M},\qquad
[\mathrm{Ag(CN)_2^-}]=0.3(3/500)=0.002\ \mathrm{M}.
$$

The key repeats the three supplied half-reactions and standard potentials below this calculation; they are the same Zn, Au and Ag reactions and $-1.26,-0.60,-0.31\ \mathrm{V}$ values above.

$$
\mathrm{Au^++2CN^-\longrightarrow[Au(CN)_2]^-},\qquad
K_f=\frac{[\mathrm{Au(CN)_2^-}]}{[\mathrm{Au^+}][\mathrm{CN^-}]^2}=4\times10^{28}.
$$

The 99 mol% condition is

$$
\frac{99}{100}=\frac{[\mathrm{Au(CN)_2^-}]}{[\mathrm{Au^+}]+[\mathrm{Au(CN)_2^-}]}.
$$

Thus $100[\mathrm{Au(CN)_2^-}]=99[\mathrm{Au^+}]+99[\mathrm{Au(CN)_2^-}]$ and $[\mathrm{Au^+}]=[\mathrm{Au(CN)_2^-}]/99$. Substitution gives

$$
4\times10^{28}=99/[\mathrm{CN^-}]^2,\qquad [\mathrm{CN^-}]=5\times10^{-14}.
$$

problems.title: Problem 6
problems.statement: Unlike carbon, tin can increase its coordination number beyond four. Like carbon it forms $\mathrm{SnCl_4}$.

sections.title: Tin geometries and spectroscopy

parts.statement:
Draw two alternative geometries for $\mathrm{SnCl_4}$.

Lewis acids such as $\mathrm{SnCl_4}$ react with Lewis bases such as chloride or amines. With chloride the following reactions occur:

$$
\mathrm{SnCl_4+Cl^-\longrightarrow SnCl_5^-},\qquad
\mathrm{SnCl_4+2Cl^-\longrightarrow SnCl_6^{2-}}.
$$
Draw three alternative geometries for $\mathrm{SnCl_5^-}$.
Use Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory to predict which geometry is likely to be preferred for $\mathrm{SnCl_5^-}$.
Draw three alternative geometries for $\mathrm{SnCl_6^{2-}}$.

Use VSEPR theory to predict which is likely to be preferred for $\mathrm{SnCl_6^{2-}}$.

A solution of $\mathrm{SnCl_6^{2-}}$ as the tetrabutylammonium salt was examined by negative-ion electrospray mass spectrometry (ESMS). It gives one peak at $m/z=295$. Assume only $^{120}\mathrm{Sn}$ and $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$ are observed.

Write the empirical formula for the tin-containing species detected.

A solution of $\mathrm{SnBr_6^{2-}}$ as the tetrabutylammonium salt gives one negative-ion ESMS peak at $m/z=515$. Assume only $^{120}\mathrm{Sn}$ and $^{79}\mathrm{Br}$ are observed.

Write the formula for the tin-containing species detected.

An equimolar mixture of the two salts gives six major species (Fig. 1).

![](p6-fig1)

Write the empirical formula for each of the four new species.

$^1\mathrm{H}$ and $^{13}\mathrm{C}$ NMR spectroscopy detect separate signals for protons and carbon nuclei in different environments. Signals are on a dimensionless parts-per-million scale relative to an agreed reference. Similarly, $^{119}\mathrm{Sn}$ NMR gives a signal for each tin atom in a different environment. The chloride salt gives one signal at $-732$ ppm relative to tetramethyltin, $\mathrm{Me_4Sn}$. The bromide salt's signal is stated in the prose as **2064 ppm**. At $60\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ the equimolar mixture gives seven peaks (Fig. 2).

![](p6-fig2)

Write the empirical formula for the species giving the peaks listed on the answer template.

Cooling to $-30\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ changes the spectrum to ten peaks (Fig. 3).

![](p6-fig3)
Draw the geometries of the four tin-containing species giving peaks at $-1092,-1115,-1322,-1336$ ppm at $-30\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

problems.title: Problem 7
problems.statement:
The structures needed to read the question are shown in the answer template. The fungus *Aspergillus nidulans* produces two isomeric aromatic lactones (cyclic esters), **A** and **B**, $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{10}O_4}$. Each dissolves in cold aqueous NaOH but not aqueous $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ and gives a violet colour with aqueous $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$. **A** with $\mathrm{CH_3I/K_2CO_3}$ gives **C**, $\mathrm{C_{11}H_{12}O_4}$, whose $^1\mathrm{H}$ NMR shows three non-identical methyl groups, one bonded directly to an aromatic ring. Selective demethylation with $\mathrm{BCl_3}$ followed by aqueous work-up gives **D**, a new isomer of **A**. Its NMR clearly shows an intramolecularly hydrogen-bonded hydroxyl at $\delta=11.8$ ppm.

![](p7-fig1)

**D** was synthesized as follows. Phenol **E** was methylated with $\mathrm{MeI/K_2CO_3}$ to **F**, $\mathrm{C_9H_{12}O_2}$, then reduced with lithium in liquid ammonia and 2-methylpropan-2-ol to a symmetrical unconjugated diene **G**. Reaction with $\mathrm{KNH_2}$ in liquid ammonia and aqueous work-up conjugates the diene to only one product **H**. Ozonolysis with non-reductive work-up affords, among other products, ketoester **I**. **H** undergoes a Diels–Alder reaction with dimethyl but-2-ynedioate **J**, giving **K**, $\mathrm{C_{15}H_{20}O_6}$. Heating expels ethene and gives aromatic ester **L**. Basic hydrolysis and acidification give **M**, $\mathrm{C_{11}H_{12}O_6}$; heating under vacuum gives **N**, $\mathrm{C_{11}H_{10}O_5}$. Reduction with $\mathrm{NaBH_4}$ in dimethylformamide gives **C** and an isomeric lactone **O**, also obtained by methylating **B**.
